facts.value: Appendix 1 Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 - 2029/30, a 20-page standalone strategy paper taken to Council on 26 January 2026. Adviser Arlingclose. The paper carries the balance sheet forecast, liability benchmark, borrowing strategy, treasury investment strategy, prudential indicators, Arlingclose December 2025 rate forecast and the 31/12/25 portfolio position. Companion Appendix 3 Non-Treasury Investment Strategy 2026/27 - 2029/30 (doc 25396, 7 pages) also held on disk, covering service loans, commercial property and total exposure indicators. Covering Cabinet/Council report NOT held.
facts.note: Both PDFs on disk are appendices. Neither carries a report author block, a Contact Officer line, or an S151 signature. Section 1.83 (p.16) refers to 'the Chief Financial Officer' without a name. No officer contact published in either appendix. Adviser Arlingclose named at §1.13 (p.3) and §1.22 of Appendix 3 (p.5).

facts.value: External borrowing £176.70m at 31/12/25, 100% PWLB at weighted average 3.94%. Total other long-term liabilities £0.00m. Total treasury investments £40.00m at 31/12/25, entirely in Money Market Funds at weighted 3.87%. Net debt £136.70m

source.title: Appendix 1 (25394) Appendix B - Existing Investment & Debt Portfolio Position, p.20
Appendix 1 (25394) Table 1 - Balance sheet summary and forecast, pp.3-4

facts.note: HRA-dominant book. HRA CFR rises £164.19m → £185.73m as the housing investment programme runs, then holds flat from 27/28. GF CFR walks steadily down from £35.80m (26/27 estimate) to £32.21m (29/30). §1.19 (p.4) cites MyPad (Northwood) and Rykneld Homes Ltd loans, plus capital programme commitments, as the drivers of rising CFR.

External borrowing rises by £27.82m across the forecast (161.30 → 189.12); balance-sheet reserves fall £11.49m (50.06 → 38.57) over the same period. The two together fund the £18.58m rise in Loans CFR (199.36 → 217.69, with a peak at £218.44 in 27/28). §1.27 (p.6) plans up to £18.60m of new borrowing in 2026/27; authorised limit £224.18m.

Internal borrowing runs off £38.06m → £28.57m (a £9.49m reduction) as balance-sheet reserves shrink and external borrowing rises to keep pace with CFR. This is a relatively small and shrinking cushion compared with most other councils we have read -- see the LB comparison in the balance_sheet_identity fact below.

source.title: Appendix 1 (25394) Table 2 - Prudential Indicator: Liability benchmark, p.5

facts.note: External borrowing vs LB by year -- 31/3/25 +£2.00m (over), 31/3/26 -£0.29m, 31/3/27 -£0.82m, 31/3/28 -£0.63m, 31/3/29 -£0.44m, 31/3/30 -£0.25m. External borrowing tracks the benchmark to within £1m in every year of the forecast -- the internal-borrowing space that most councils use as a buffer above the LB is almost fully consumed here. Long-term LB chart on p.5 assumes £19.71m of capital expenditure funded by borrowing over the report term, MRP on 50-year asset life, and slightly declining income/expenditure/reserves (§1.23).

facts.value: New long-term borrowing assumed at 5.50% for budget-setting; new treasury investments at 3.25% (§1.16 p.3). Short-term rates falling and expected to fall further; likely to be more cost effective medium-term to use internal resources or borrow short-term (§1.29 p.6). PWLB historically only source but will consider banks, pensions, LAs, bonds (§1.31 p.7). National Wealth Fund on approved-source list (§1.34 p.7). Council intends to avoid buying investment assets primarily for yield to retain PWLB access (§1.31 p.7). Debt rescheduling considered where cost savings or risk reduction arise (§1.38 p.8)

source.title: Appendix 1 (25394) §1.27-1.38 Borrowing Strategy, pp.6-8; §1.16 Budget assumptions, p.3

facts.note: 5.50% assumption sits between today's 10yr PWLB Certainty (5.28%, gilt 4.48+0.80) and 20yr Certainty (5.93%, gilt 5.13+0.80). Below Arlingclose's own central-case Dec 2025 forecast for 20yr Certainty (Mar-26 4.85+0.80 = 5.65%). Cautious and reasonable. Forward starting loans mentioned (§1.32) as an option to lock rate without cost of carry. §1.30 confirms Arlingclose will provide cost of carry and breakeven analysis.

facts.value: None held. §1.36 (p.7) states verbatim: 'The Council doesn't hold or intend to hold any LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans.' Loan book is 100% PWLB per Appendix B (p.20)

source.title: Appendix 1 (25394) §1.36 LOBOs, p.7; Appendix B p.20

facts.note: Unusually explicit statement. Many strategies leave LOBO absence implicit or omit the sentence entirely; naming it removes any ambiguity for readers.

facts.value: Arlingclose central case (December 2025 forecast, Appendix A p.19). Official Bank Rate 4.00% (current) → 3.75% (Dec-25) → 3.50% (Mar-26) → 3.25% (Jun-26) → 3.25% (held through Sep-28). 20yr gilt 5.13% (current) → 4.90% (Dec-25) → 4.85% (Mar-26) → 4.75-4.85% through the forecast. 10yr gilt 4.48% (current) → 4.35% (Mar-26) → 4.25% steady. 50yr gilt 4.73% → 4.50% → 4.45-4.50%. PWLB Certainty = Gilt + 0.80%; HRA = Gilt + 0.40%

source.title: Appendix 1 (25394) Appendix A - Arlingclose Economic & Interest Rate Forecast, pp.18-19

facts.note: Forecast dated December 2025. Central case: further 25bp cut in Dec-25 to 3.75%, then to 3.25% by Q2 2026 held through the forecast. Downside risks weighted. Long-end gilt yields expected 'to remain broadly stable on average, though with continued volatility, and to end the forecast period marginally lower' (§1.14). Six/seven weeks between forecast date and Council decision on 26 January 2026.

facts.value: Interest rate risk limit (§1.73 p.14): symmetric ±£1.72m one-year revenue impact of 1% rate change. Liquidity risk (§1.72): total cash within 3 months £10.00m. Credit risk (§1.71): portfolio average credit rating target <5.00. Maturity structure LIMITS only (§1.75 p.14) -- under 12m 0-20%, 12-24m 0-20%, 24m-5y 0-40%, 5-10y 0-40%, 10y+ 0-90%. Long-term investments limit (§1.77 p.15) £20m in every year. Authorised limit for borrowing £224.18m (§1.27 p.6)

source.title: Appendix 1 (25394) §1.70-1.77 Treasury Management Prudential Indicators, pp.13-15

facts.note: £1.72m interest rate limit is 1% of £172m -- almost exactly the 31/3/26 external borrowing forecast, so the limit is effectively at the notional cap that the whole book could reprice against in a year. The paper does NOT print an actual maturity distribution of the current £176.70m book against these buckets -- only the limits. The Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue prudential indicator is NOT in either paper on disk; presumably in the covering report. MRP Policy Statement is NOT in either paper on disk.

facts.value: General Fund investment income budget 2026/27 £0.40m. HRA investment income budget 2026/27 £0.15m on £15m average portfolio at 3.75%. HRA debt interest budget 2026/27 £6.81m on £178.61m average debt portfolio at 4.05% (§1.84 p.16). Investment reserves available to cover losses £31.27m at 31/3/26, £30.77m at 31/3/27 (§1.65 p.13)
facts.note: HRA average debt portfolio £178.61m at 4.05% is c.£2m above the current £176.70m PWLB book, and 11bp above the 3.94% weighted rate at 31/12/25. Consistent with the £18.60m of new borrowing planned at ~5.50% blending into the book across the year, weighted toward HRA.

officer.body:
Dear [RECIPIENT NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy that went to Council on 26 January. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your strategy is unusually clear on some points that other papers leave implicit, and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The first thing that stood out is Table 1 read against Table 2. Your external borrowing walks 161.30 → 172.00 → 177.70 → 186.11 → 187.62 → 189.12 across the forecast; your liability benchmark walks 159.30 → 172.29 → 178.52 → 186.74 → 188.06 → 189.37. The two lines sit within a pound in every year of the forecast — £2m over at 31/3/25, then £0.29m under at 31/3/26, and inside a million-pound margin thereafter. That is an unusual shape for a district book. Most of the strategies we've read carry a real internal-borrowing buffer above the benchmark, funded by reserves above the liquidity floor, and either run it down as a live decision or leave it in place. Your Table 1 shows that internal borrowing walks £38.06m → £28.57m as reserves fall from £50.06m to £38.57m, so the buffer is being used up rather than held back. Paragraph 1.27 sets out the £18.60m of new borrowing planned in 2026/27, which is what keeps the external line moving up with the benchmark. Not a criticism — just a shape a treasurer would recognise from the page and worth flagging.

The second observation is on paragraph 1.16 read alongside Arlingclose's own forecast in Appendix A. The 5.50% budget rate you've set for new long-term borrowing sits below every reference point we can find. Today's PWLB Certainty rates — gilt yield plus 80 basis points on Arlingclose's own spread — are roughly 4.72% at 5 years, 5.28% at 10 years, 5.93% at 20 years and 5.53% at 50 years. Your adviser's own central-case Mar-26 forecast has 20-year Certainty landing at about 5.65%. So 5.50% is between today's 10-year and 20-year Certainty and about 15 basis points below your adviser's own Q1-26 20-year central case. Cautious against both, and worth a checkpoint against whichever bucket you actually draw in — 5.50% for a 10-year draw is comfortable headroom, for a 20-year draw it's already 43bp inside today's curve.

Third, briefly, and it's the kind of clarity that we notice because most strategies don't do it. Paragraph 1.36 says outright that the Council doesn't hold or intend to hold any LOBO loans. Twelve LOBO calls have gone through the sector this year that we can see, so it's an active market again, and a reader of a strategy that leaves the position implicit has to check elsewhere. Naming an absence is a small thing but it lets a reader stop asking.

Where it would be quickest to look on our side is pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, where the liability benchmark chart runs live against the current forward curve. It's the natural companion to your Table 2 and the p.5 chart in the paper. The gap between the two curves is the space where a treasurer decides whether the £18.60m of 26/27 borrowing goes short, long, forward-starting or in tranches, and it moves every day.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway becomes central to how the whole strategy is framed. Your section 1.21-1.26 already sets the benchmark out and prints the chart. An interactive version tied to our rate feeds is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — useful because the p.5 chart's long-dated tail runs into the 2070s, and seeing how the market's forward curve moves against that pathway is easier live than in a snapshot.

On training, three fit the paper. The liability benchmark pathway is the natural complement to your section 1.21-1.26. PWLB rates — reading the curve alongside an adviser's central case picks up the paragraph 1.16 question. And Investment strategy for HRA-dominant districts is closest to the shape of your book, where the HRA CFR carries 83% of the underlying borrowing need today and 85% by 2030. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are open to the whole team.

And if any of it turns out to be useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
